verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r13 cards against the live .md versions of the official pages, downloaded 2026-10-13. Every source URL returns 200, and the release notes show 9.0-series as the current stable release, so the 9.0 pin holds. 10 cards pass. Supporting quotes for the passing cards:
- 01: write-operations-atomicity says "the modification of each document is atomic, but the operation as a whole is not atomic".
- 03: production-consideration says "standalone deployments do not support transactions".
- 04: Session.abortTransaction says changes "are discarded without ever becoming visible".
- 05: transactions says "Transactions that contain read operations must use read preference primary".
- 06: transactions says "Setting write concerns for the individual write operations inside a transaction returns an error".
- 07: read-concern-snapshot says "provides its guarantees only if the transaction commits with write concern majority".
- 08: production-consideration, In-progress Transactions and Write Conflicts section, supports it verbatim.
- 10: transactions-in-applications says "Starting in MongoDB 6.2, the server does not retry the transaction if it receives a TransactionTooLargeForCache error". I also checked the server source (error_labels.cpp): TransactionTooLargeForCache does not get the TransientTransactionError label, so the driver callback API does not retry it either and the False answer holds.
- 11: the parameters page lists maxConcurrentMultiDocumentTransactions as "New in version 9.0 (also available in 8.3.7)", default 10000, rejecting with TooManyOpenTransactions.
- 12: transactions-in-applications says to retry the whole transaction for TransientTransactionError and only the commit for UnknownTransactionCommitResult.
- No duplicates with other sections. The nearest is sr14-03 (snapshot reads outside transactions), which is a different fact from sr13-07.

Minor points, not flagged:
- sr13-11: "can cap" is a hedged capability claim that a guesser would likely answer True. Its explanation says "An enabled server-wide limit", which suggests the cap is opt-in, but it is on by default (default 10000; 0 disables it). Consider "In MongoDB 9.0, mongod rejects new external-client transactions with TooManyOpenTransactions once its open-transaction cap is reached." The volatility note says "MongoDB 9.0 adds" this; it was also backported to 8.3.7.
- sr13-04 is an easy, borderline basic-isolation card but is correct.
- Keeping both replacements True keeps the section at 6 True and 6 False.

Prompt rules checked: the 9.0 pin, the 9.0 server-side external-client transaction limit, "do not claim transactions prohibit collection creation" (the transactions page confirms implicit and explicit creation) and the retry scope that depends on the error are all confirmed on official pages. I found no prompt rule wrong for r13. One documentation quirk: the production-consideration page says transactions need "a multiple node replica set", although single-node replica sets do support transactions. No r13 card relies on that sentence.

verdicts.notes:
I opened the source URL of all 12 r14 cards. Every page loads as a 9.0 (Current) official manual page: read-concern-local, read-concern-majority, read-concern-snapshot, read-concern-linearizable, write-concern, core/replica-set-write-concern and core/causal-consistency-read-write-concerns. Each page supports its card, including the fact the explanation gives for each false statement.

Evidence for the cards that pass:
- 01: local "returns data from the instance with no guarantee that the data has been written to a majority".
- 02: "To fulfill read concern majority, the node returns data from this view". This is a per-node in-memory majority-commit view. The Cassandra-style quorum-read misconception is realistic.
- 03: outside transactions, snapshot "is available on primaries and secondaries for find, aggregate, distinct (on unsharded collections)" and reads majority-committed data.
- 04: "Linearizable read concern guarantees only apply if read operations specify a query filter that uniquely identifies a single document."
- 05: "w: 1 only requires acknowledgment from the primary".
- 06: "Secondaries do not need to be voting members to meet the write concern threshold."
- 08: "MongoDB does not undo successful data modifications performed before the write concern exceeded the wtimeout time limit."
- 09: wtimeout applies "after the operation succeeds on the primary".
- 10: "Starting in MongoDB 8.0, { w: \"majority\" } writes return an acknowledgment after a majority of data-bearing members durably write the oplog entry. Members then asynchronously apply..." The statement correctly carries the "In MongoDB 9.0" pin.
- 11: arbiter formula and PSA example give { w: 1 }.
- 12: majority/majority is the only combination that guarantees all four causal guarantees, "even in circumstances (such as with a network partition)".

Minor observations, not flagged:
- 08 and 09 both test wtimeout (retention versus timing phase). These are distinct facts, but two of the 12 cards in the section go to one option.
- 12 is close to the definition of causal consistency. It passes because the majority/majority condition is the point being taught.

Overlap check against r13, r15 and r16: no duplicates found. sr15-11 covers w:1 rollback, so the replacement for sr14-07 deliberately avoids rollback. sr15-02 (asynchronous replay) does not give away sr14-10.

Prompt rules checked for this section: the 9.0 pin, the 8.0 majority-acknowledgment change, wtimeout not rolling back writes, the arbiter-dependent implicit default, and causal read-your-writes requiring majority read and write concerns all match the current official pages. I found no wrong prompt rule for r14. True/false balance stays 6/6 with the suggested false replacement.

flagged.evidence: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-elections/ : "Secondaries with higher priority call elections sooner and are more likely to win. However, a lower priority instance can be elected as primary for brief periods, even if a higher priority secondary is available." and "Replica set members continue to call elections until the highest priority member available becomes primary."
flagged.problem: The statement has no 'always' or 'guarantees', so it reads as a general description: 'the highest-priority available member becomes primary before a lower-priority one'. That is the normal tendency the docs describe (higher priority calls elections sooner and is more likely to win). The answer is False only if the player reads it as a guarantee. An expert could defend True. The prompt also says to avoid election-time guarantees, and the card depends on exactly that unstated guarantee.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep answer False and make the guarantee explicit. Statement: "In a replica set, an available higher-priority secondary blocks a lower-priority member from winning an election." Explanation: "Priority is best effort. A lower-priority member can be elected primary briefly while a higher-priority secondary is available, and that secondary then calls elections until it takes over."

flagged.evidence: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-rollbacks/ : "Data may be rolled back if the primary steps down before the write operations have replicated to any of the secondaries." and "By default, when a rollback occurs, MongoDB writes the rollback data to BSON files."
flagged.problem: The answer (False) is correct. The explanation says the former primary "discards" the divergent write, which suggests the data is lost. By default MongoDB reverts the write from the data set and keeps it in rollback BSON files under <dbpath>/rollback, where an administrator can review and recover it.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep the statement (False). Explanation: "A {w:1} write can roll back if the primary steps down before secondaries replicate it. The rejoining member reverts the write and by default saves it to rollback BSON files."

verdicts.notes:
All 12 r15 cards were checked against the live MongoDB 9.0 (Current) manual pages. Every source URL loads and is official. Balance is 6 True (01, 02, 04, 05, 07, 08) and 6 False (03, 06, 09, 10, 11, 12). The two fixes above keep that balance.

Passed, with the quotes that settle them:
- 01: replica-set-primary says "The primary is the only member in the replica set that receives write operations."
- 02: replica-set-secondary says "a secondary applies operations from the primary's oplog to its own data set in an asynchronous process."
- 03: replica-set-oplog says "If write operations do not modify any data or fail, they do not create oplog entries." updateMany is not a retryable write, so the retryable no-op exception does not apply.
- 04: read-preference says "Default mode. All operations read from the current replica set primary."
- 05: read-preference says "primaries and secondaries are treated equivalently" in nearest mode.
- 06: read-preference says "If no secondaries are available, then this read operation produces an error or exception." Minor wording issue: "By default" suggests a setting exists that turns on a primary fallback for secondary mode, but there is none. That fallback is a different mode, secondaryPreferred. Consider dropping "By default".
- 07: read-preference-tags says "MongoDB tries each document in succession until a match is found ... the remaining tag sets are ignored."
- 08: replica-set-elections says a member "that can communicate with a majority of the voting nodes (including itself) holds an election" and "The first member to receive the majority of votes becomes the new PRIMARY."
- 09: replica-set-arbiter says "an arbiter does not have a copy of the data set."
- 10: replica-set-priority-0-member says such a member "cannot become primary" yet does "vote in elections".

Possible overlap, not flagged: sr14-10's explanation says "Secondary application proceeds asynchronously", which is close to sr15-02's fact. The two cards test different facts (what majority acknowledgment means versus how secondaries replicate), so they are not duplicates.

The prompt rules for r15 (MongoDB 9.0 pin, stale secondary reads, arbiters vote without storing data, elections need a voting majority, avoid election-time guarantees) are consistent with the current docs; I found no prompt rule wrong for this section. Card 12 breaks the prompt's own rule against election-time guarantees, which is why it is flagged.

flagged.evidence: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-shard-key-indexes/ : sh.shardCollection() creates the shard-key index on an empty collection; for a populated collection 'you must create the index first', and the index must be on the shard key or a compound index with the shard key as a prefix.
flagged.problem: The answer is right, but the wording gives it away. A 'supporting index' for a {tenant:1} shard key starts with {tenant:1} by definition, so the statement 'requires the supporting index to start with {tenant:1}' is nearly circular. A player can answer True from the wording without knowing the populated-versus-empty rule or the compound-prefix rule. The sentence is also awkward ('requires a populated collection's supporting index to start with').
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep answer TRUE. Statement: "To shard a populated collection on {tenant:1}, an existing {tenant:1,region:1} index can serve as its shard-key index." Explanation: "A populated collection needs a shard-key index before sh.shardCollection() runs, and a compound index with the shard key as prefix qualifies. Only an empty collection gets that index built automatically."

flagged.evidence: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-choose-a-shard-key/ : 'Where possible, choose a shard key with high cardinality. A shard key with low cardinality reduces the effectiveness of horizontal scaling in the cluster.' and 'A cardinality of 7 means there can be no more than 7 chunks ... adding more than seven shards would not provide any benefit.'
flagged.problem: Strawman. Anyone who has read the shard-key guidance knows MongoDB does not 'favor low cardinality' for scaling, so almost nobody who studied would answer True. The card also only tells the player that the guidance points the other way. It does not test the mechanism behind it: each value lives in one chunk, which caps the number of effective shards.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep answer FALSE. Statement: "Adding more shards than a shard key has distinct values spreads that sharded collection's data further." Explanation: "Each shard-key value lives in at most one chunk, so a key with 7 distinct values allows at most 7 chunks and 7 useful shards. MongoDB recommends high-cardinality shard keys."

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r16 cards. Every source URL loads, is official and shows Database Manual 9.0 (Current). The section is balanced at 6 true and 6 false, and both suggested fixes keep that balance.

Cards that passed, with the quote that settles each one:
- sr16-01: query-router page, "mongos uses the shard key value to locate the chunk whose range includes the shard key value and directs the query at the shard containing that chunk".
- sr16-02: config-servers page, "Config servers store the metadata ... the list of chunks on every shard and the ranges that define the chunks", and "The mongos instances cache this data".
- sr16-05: frequency is described as a chunk bottleneck on the choose-a-shard-key page.
- sr16-06: hashed-sharding page, "Hashed keys are ideal for shard keys with fields that change monotonically".
- sr16-07: data-partitioning page, "Each chunk has inclusive lower and exclusive upper limits based on the shard key".
- sr16-08: balancer page, "monitors the amount of data on each shard for each sharded collection".
- sr16-09: change-a-shard-key page, "refine a shard key by adding a suffix field or fields" versus "change a collection's shard key entirely and reshard".
- sr16-10: change-shard-key-value page requires mongos, a transaction or retryable write, and equality on the full shard key. This still holds in 9.0; the 7.1 relaxation for updateOne without a shard key does not cover changing a shard-key value. _id stays immutable, and updateOne() is a listed method.
- sr16-11: shard-key-indexes page allows a unique compound index on a ranged sharded collection when the shard key is its prefix. Unique hashed indexes are not allowed, and the statement correctly says "ranged".
- sr16-12: "Sharded clusters do not enforce the uniqueness constraint on _id fields across the cluster when the _id field is not the shard key."

I found no duplicates within the deck. sr2-12 (unique _id index on an unsharded collection) versus sr16-12 is the split the prompt assigns between r2 and r16. sr7-08 ($merge to a sharded collection) and sr8-10 ($lookup with a sharded foreign collection) rest on different facts.

Prompt rules: I confirmed the r16 rules on official pages and found none wrong:
- the 9.0 pin matches the current manual;
- sh.disableAutoSplit says "Starting in MongoDB 6.0.3, automatic chunk splitting is not performed ... Auto-splitting commands still exist, but do not perform an operation";
- balancing is data-based, with a migration threshold of 3x the range size (default 128MB);
- refine appends and reshard replaces;
- shard-key values are changeable except _id;
- _id uniqueness is per shard.

One minor point: several r16 cards cite official pages outside the prompt's r16 source list (query-router, config-servers, shard-key-indexes, hashed-sharding, change-a-shard-key, change-shard-key-value). These are current official manual pages and support the cards, so I did not flag it.

duplicates.why: Both cards test one read-pattern distinction. Data fetched together with its parent favors embedding (sr12-01, true), and an entity queried on its own favors referencing (sr12-03, false). The prompt says the two sides of one distinction are one fact. sr12-01 is the weaker card: it shares the 'MongoDB favors embedding bounded ...' template with sr12-02, and the word 'bounded' marks it true.

Unbounded embedded child arrays are risky (sr12-05, true), and that same fact makes 'favor embedding for a very large number of children' false (sr12-06). Knowing one answer gives the other. The section spec also lists them as one item ('high cardinality and unbounded array growth'). sr12-05 is close to a truism because the word 'Unbounded' already signals the risk.

sr11-05 says an index with partialFilterExpression:{active:true} has no entries for active:false documents. Since uniqueness is enforced through index entries, that directly answers sr11-08: the partial unique index does not reject duplicates among inactive documents. sr11-05 is also close to a definition card, because the filter's meaning gives its answer.

conflictGroups.name: objectid-time-and-origin
conflictGroups.why: sr1-09's explanation names 'values generated in the same second' and 'differences between client clocks'. That reveals the embedded timestamp (sr1-08, true) and that clients generate ObjectIds (sr2-09, true).

conflictGroups.name: bson-numeric-types
conflictGroups.why: sr1-03's statement ('a BSON long whose value also fits in int') and its explanation ('preserves the BSON long type ... even for small values') show that int and long are distinct stored types, which answers sr1-04.

conflictGroups.name: bson-versus-json
conflictGroups.why: sr1-03 and sr1-04 talk about BSON types and Extended JSON wrappers. That makes 'MongoDB stores plain JSON text' (sr1-02, false) trivially false.

conflictGroups.name: validation-existing-documents
conflictGroups.why: sr2-06 (moderate skips updates to existing invalid documents) assumes that invalid documents survive when a validator is enabled. That hints that enabling strict does not check existing data (sr2-05, false).

conflictGroups.name: id-immutability
conflictGroups.why: sr16-10 explicitly limits shard-key value changes to 'non-_id' fields, which signals that _id cannot be changed (sr2-11, false).

conflictGroups.name: id-index-uniqueness-scope
conflictGroups.why: sr2-12 limits the unique _id index to 'ordinary unsharded' collections, and sr16-11 shows that sharded unique indexes depend on a shard-key prefix. Both hint that _id uniqueness across shards is not enforced by the default index (sr16-12, false).

conflictGroups.name: ordered-insertmany
conflictGroups.why: sr3-03's explanation (successful inserts before the error remain stored) and sr3-02's explanation (ordered:true is the default and stops the remaining inserts) answer each other. sr3-04's explanation contrasts ordered:false with that default.

conflictGroups.name: missing-field-matching
conflictGroups.why: sr4-07 ($nin matches missing fields) and sr11-04 (explicit null and a missing field give the same index key) both teach that a missing field behaves like null. That strongly hints that {status:null} also matches missing fields (sr4-08, false).

conflictGroups.name: array-equality-semantics
conflictGroups.why: sr5-04's explanation (whole-array equality compares the element sequence) and sr10-05's explanation (fetch to verify the complete array) cross-inform each other. Both contrast with $all and with scalar element matching, which also allow extra elements.

conflictGroups.name: elemmatch-single-element
conflictGroups.why: sr10-04's explanation (joining predicates under $elemMatch lets MongoDB intersect bounds) relies on the conditions binding to one element, which is sr5-07's answer.

conflictGroups.name: positional-dollar-query-binding
conflictGroups.why: sr6-10's explanation (MongoDB derives the array position from the query match) hints that positional $ projection returns the first element matched by the query (sr5-09).

conflictGroups.name: pipeline-stage-sequence
conflictGroups.why: sr7-01's explanation (later stages evaluate the shape produced by earlier stages) directly implies that a $limit placed before $sort cannot use the later sort's ranking (sr7-05, false).

conflictGroups.name: aggregation-persistence
conflictGroups.why: sr7-07 and sr7-08 present $out and $merge as the stages that write. sr6-12 shows that persistent reshaping goes through an update pipeline. Together they give away that aggregate() with $set alone does not persist (sr7-09, false).

conflictGroups.name: aggregation-memory-limits
conflictGroups.why: sr7-11's explanation ('even when disk spilling is enabled') confirms that per-stage spilling exists (sr7-10, true). sr7-10's 'stage memory allowance' hints at a separate operation-level cap.

conflictGroups.name: sharded-collection-acceptance-template
conflictGroups.why: Both use the same true template ('In a sharded cluster, the $X stage accepts/can write a sharded collection'). Dealt together, one answers the other by analogy.

conflictGroups.name: unwind-output-shape
conflictGroups.why: sr8-12 says $unwind 'retains a document', and its explanation says the path stays absent 'in the output'. That shows $unwind emits documents, not bare values (sr8-11, false).

conflictGroups.name: unspecified-result-order
conflictGroups.why: sr3-08, sr8-02 and sr10-11 all teach that order is unspecified unless you sort explicitly, and each explanation says 'add a $sort' or 'explicit sort'. sr8-05's explanation ('Sort before grouping to establish the desired array order') repeats the lesson. Seeing one makes the others' false 'default order' claims guessable.

conflictGroups.name: text-search-string-semantics
conflictGroups.why: sr10-10 contrasts 'unquoted terms', and its explanation says unquoted terms use OR. That hints that quoted words mean something else, a phrase (sr10-12, true).

conflictGroups.name: text-index-prerequisite
conflictGroups.why: sr10-08 says a text index serves $text queries, which suggests that a regular ascending index does not (sr10-09, false).

conflictGroups.name: partial-index-scope
conflictGroups.why: All four use the same email/active:true partial index. sr11-05 and sr11-06's explanation ('the partial index could omit valid results') reveal that inactive documents are absent from the index, which answers sr11-08. sr11-07's setup also confirms that a non-key filter field is valid.

conflictGroups.name: embed-versus-reference-template
conflictGroups.why: These are four 'MongoDB favors embedding ...' cards. The bounded/fetched-together ones are true and the independent/high-cardinality ones are false. Dealt together they answer each other.

conflictGroups.name: unbounded-child-growth
conflictGroups.why: The unbounded-array risk (sr12-05, true) directly answers 'favor embedding for very many children' (sr12-06, false).

conflictGroups.name: computed-pattern
conflictGroups.why: sr12-08's statement ('Periodic Computed pattern refreshes keep stored summaries ...') reveals that the pattern stores derived results (sr12-07, true). sr12-07 in turn frames the stored value as a snapshot that can go stale.

conflictGroups.name: application-managed-patterns
conflictGroups.why: All three are false through the same 'the server does the application's job' trick (propagating copies, moving overflow, a collection-level version option). Each explanation says the application handles it, which gives away the others.

conflictGroups.name: transaction-topology
conflictGroups.why: sr13-02 and the other r13 statements consistently say 'on a replica set'. Next to them, sr13-03's standalone claim (false) is easy to guess.

conflictGroups.name: transaction-write-concern-scope
conflictGroups.why: sr13-07 describes a transaction whose commit carries the write concern (w:1 commit), and its explanation names commit with majority write concern. That hints the transaction, not each operation, owns write concern (sr13-06).

conflictGroups.name: async-secondary-application
conflictGroups.why: sr15-02 (secondaries replay the oplog asynchronously) and sr14-10's explanation ('Secondary application proceeds asynchronously') answer each other. Majority acknowledgment does not mean the secondaries have applied the write.

conflictGroups.name: w1-acknowledgment-durability
conflictGroups.why: sr15-11's explanation (a {w:1} write rolls back if secondaries had not replicated it) reveals that w:1 is primary-only acknowledgment (sr14-05, true).

conflictGroups.name: wtimeout-semantics
conflictGroups.why: sr14-08's explanation ('ends the acknowledgment wait. Successful changes on the primary remain') answers sr14-09 (false). sr14-09's explanation ('starts after the write succeeds on the primary') hints at sr14-08 (true).

conflictGroups.name: arbiter-holds-no-data
conflictGroups.why: sr14-11's explanation contrasts 'data-bearing voting members' with the arbiter. That reveals arbiters store no data (sr15-09, false).

conflictGroups.name: read-preference-mode-membership
conflictGroups.why: sr15-05's explanation (nearest considers primaries and secondaries together) contrasts with the secondary mode. sr15-06's explanation (secondary fails instead of falling back) contrasts with the modes that include the primary.

conflictGroups.name: shard-key-value-distribution
conflictGroups.why: sr16-05 (frequently repeated shard-key values concentrate load) strongly hints that favoring low cardinality is wrong (sr16-04, false).

scan.tells:
Average statement lengths are balanced in every section. The largest true-versus-false gap is 4.5 characters (r13, true longer), and the deck-wide averages are true 92.3 and false 91.7. The word tells are the following.
